1. Core Clinical Tension: A 26-year-old underweight female undergoing second-line therapy for multidrug-resistant pulmonary mycobacterial disease developed acute behavioural changes, visual hallucinations, delusions, and aggression 10 days after starting a modified regimen containing cycloserine. The diagnostic dilemma lies in differentiating drug-induced neuropsychiatric toxicity from primary psychosis, central nervous system involvement, or metabolic delirium.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint occurs at the onset of acute psychosis and behavioural instability on day 10 of second-line therapy, prior to formal psychiatric rating scale assessment (BPRS), adverse drug reaction probability scoring (Naranjo algorithm), and cycloserine discontinuation.
3. Differential Distinctions: Primary psychotic disorder was considered due to prominent delusions, visual hallucinations, and aggression, but ruled out by the absence of prior psychiatric history, absence of family history, and rapid resolution within 72 hours of drug withdrawal; metabolic/organic delirium was ruled out by normal electrolytes, renal function, and thyroid function; cycloserine-induced psychosis was established by a Naranjo score of 7 and prompt clinical resolution upon stopping cycloserine.
case_prompt:
A 26-year-old female weighing 35 kg was evaluated for management of drug-resistant chronic pulmonary cavitary disease. She had previously completed a nine-month standard antimycobacterial regimen (three months of four-drug intensive therapy followed by six months of dual maintenance therapy), but subsequently developed a recurrent early-morning cough productive of mucoid sputum that worsened in the left lateral decubitus position. High-resolution computed tomography of the chest revealed multiple centrilobular nodules with a 'tree-in-bud' appearance in the right upper and middle lobes, consolidative patches with breakdown cavitations in the right upper lobe apical segment, complete collapse of the left lung with volume loss, cystic bronchiectatic changes, and mediastinal shift to the left. Due to documented resistance to first-line agents, she was initiated on a modified second-line treatment regimen consisting of bedaquiline (200 mg every other day), delamanid (100 mg twice daily), linezolid (600 mg once daily), cycloserine (500 mg once daily), clofazimine (100 mg nightly), pyridoxine (100 mg nightly), sildenafil, ferrous ascorbate, folic acid, and pantoprazole.

Ten days after starting this regimen, the patient exhibited acute behavioral changes characterized by social withdrawal, irritability, irrational speech, physical aggression, severe insomnia, refusal to eat, restlessness, and visual hallucinations accompanied by persecutory delusions. She had no prior personal or family history of psychiatric illness and no history of psychoactive substance use. On physical examination, her body weight was 35 kg; she exhibited mild pallor, generalized lymphadenopathy, and increased psychomotor activity with incoherent speech. Routine laboratory investigations revealed a hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL, while leukocyte count with differentials, serum electrolytes, blood urea, serum creatinine, urinalysis, and thyroid function tests were all within normal limits.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the florid presentation of delusions, visual hallucinations, irrational speech, and aggression, but ruled out by the lack of prior psychiatric history, absence of psychiatric family history, acute temporal onset 10 days post-drug initiation, and rapid reversibility upon drug cessation.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The patient had no prior psychiatric history, did not use any psychoactive substances, and had no family history of psychiatric or other medical conditions.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered given the patient's severe wasting (body weight 35 kg), anemia, and chronic debilitating lung disease, but ruled out by entirely normal serum electrolytes, renal function parameters, urinalysis, and thyroid function tests.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Routine investigations, including a full blood count with differentials, electrolyte levels, urea, creatinine, urinalysis, and thyroid function tests, were all within normal ranges except for the hemoglobin level of 9.2 g/dL (anemic).

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Adverse drug reaction evaluation demonstrated a Naranjo probability score of 7 and a BPRS score of 50, pointing to cycloserine-induced neurotoxicity; withdrawal of cycloserine while continuing the remaining anti-TB drugs resulted in prompt clinical recovery, with BPRS falling from 50 to 20 within 72 hours.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The BPRS score was 50, and the Naranjo algorithm score was 7, in this case suggesting probable drug-induced psychosis. Cycloserine was identified as the likely cause, and it was discontinued while the remaining anti-TB drugs were continued without modification... Within 72 hours, the BPRS score reduced from 50 to 20, indicating significant improvement in psychiatric symptoms.

editor_comments: Stanford MedCaseReasoning distillation verified. Breakpoint set on day 10 upon evaluation of acute psychosis and baseline lab review, strictly prior to Naranjo/BPRS scoring and cycloserine dechallenge. Zero pathogen spoilers in prompt. Exact verbatim quotes confirmed.
